takes.text: Rush hour: forty people in this carriage are streaming music over the same slice of radio.
So why don't you ever hear your neighbour's?
You might think pairing gives your earbuds a private channel, like an invisible wire.
There's no such thing. Yours share every channel with everyone in here.
It's one band, at two point four gigahertz, shared with café Wi-Fi and even microwave ovens.
Classic Bluetooth slices it into seventy-nine channels.
And it never stays on one. It jumps channel up to sixteen hundred times a second.
The jumps look random, but they follow a timetable your phone works out from its address and its clock.
Your earbuds work out the same one, so they're always listening in the right place at the right moment.
Still, someone else's packet will sometimes land on your channel.
So every packet starts with a name tag: a code made from your phone's address.
Your earbuds only open up for that code. Your neighbour's music carries a different one.
And sometimes two packets hit the same channel at the same instant.
Bluetooth's own rulebook calls that a strong likelihood.
They garble each other. Your earbuds don't confirm, so your phone sends it again on the next hop, milliseconds later.
And a fraction of a second of music waits in reserve, so you don't hear the gap.
Cafés add a bigger problem: Wi-Fi doesn't hop. A network camps on about twenty of those channels.
So your phone keeps score. Channels that keep failing are dropped from the timetable, though it always keeps at least twenty.
So your earbuds never had a private line.
They have their own timetable, a name tag and a second chance, up to sixteen hundred times a second.
And if you do want your neighbour's song? Newer Bluetooth can share one stream with any number of earbuds.
